meta.title: Morning Recall
meta.subtitle: Produce the answer before you look.
meta.rule: Attempt each prompt from memory first, out loud or on paper. A short answer is revealed only after you mark the card, so a blank is recoverable; the guides hold the full detail.

types.fact: Recall a discrete fact or rule. Fast. Say it, don't think it.
types.procedure: Reproduce a skeleton or sequence from blank. Write it or say it end to end.
types.spoken: Answer out loud, timed, as if in the room. Do not read notes.

prompts.prompt: How do === and Object.is differ on the two edge cases NaN and -0, and what equality do Map/Set use?
prompts.answer: === gives NaN !== NaN (false) and 0 === -0 (true); Object.is flips both, so Object.is(NaN, NaN) is true and Object.is(0, -0) is false. Map/Set use SameValueZero: NaN equals NaN, but 0 equals -0, and objects still compare by identity.

prompts.prompt: What does a shallow copy like {...o} or structuredClone each handle, and what are structuredClone's limits?
prompts.answer: Shallow copies ({...o}, [...a]) share nested references. structuredClone handles cycles, Map, Set, and Date, but cannot clone functions or DOM nodes.

prompts.prompt: Give the results and rules for: 1 + '2', '3' - 1, Boolean([]), Number(''), and typeof null.
prompts.answer: 1 + '2' is '12' (+ concatenates with a string); '3' - 1 is 2 (numeric operators coerce); Boolean([]) is true (objects are truthy); Number('') is 0; typeof null is 'object' (historical bug).

prompts.prompt: List JavaScript's complete set of falsy values, and what is x == null true for?
prompts.answer: Falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, '' (empty string), null, undefined, NaN. x == null is true only for null and undefined, making it the deliberate nullish check.

prompts.prompt: Contrast let/const versus var for scope and initialization, and why does `for (let i...) setTimeout(...)` log 0 1 2?
prompts.answer: let/const are block scoped and sit in a temporal dead zone before declaration; var is function scoped and initialized to undefined. The loop logs 0 1 2 because let creates a fresh per-iteration binding captured by each closure.

prompts.prompt: How is `this` decided for obj.f(), a bare f(), f.call(x)/f.bind(x), and an arrow function?
prompts.answer: this is set by the call site: obj.f() -> obj; bare f() -> undefined in strict/module code; f.call(x) invokes with this=x now, f.bind(x) returns a new function bound to x. Arrow functions use lexical this, which call/bind cannot change. A detached method (const m = obj.f; m()) loses its receiver.

prompts.prompt: What are the steps of `new C()`, and where do instance methods versus class field arrow functions live?
prompts.answer: new C() creates an object, sets its prototype, calls C with this bound to it, and returns the explicit object if C returns one. Instance methods live on C.prototype (shared); field arrow functions are per-instance. Object.hasOwn(o,k) tests only own properties.

prompts.prompt: State the array-method traps for reduce, sort, find, splice, and slice.
prompts.answer: reduce: always pass an initial value; sort: mutates and defaults to string order; find/findIndex: return undefined vs -1 when absent; splice: mutates in place and returns removed items; slice: end is exclusive and it copies. Non-mutating twins are toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, and with.

prompts.prompt: How do for...in, Object.keys, and for...of differ, and how do you build a 2-D grid without aliasing rows?
prompts.answer: for...in includes enumerable inherited keys; Object.keys/values/entries return own enumerable string-keyed properties (symbols need getOwnPropertySymbols); for...of iterates iterables. Build a grid with Array.from({length: m}, () => Array(n).fill(0)) because Array(m).fill(Array(n)) aliases one shared row.

prompts.prompt: Why does string length not equal character count, and what does [...s] iterate?
prompts.answer: length counts UTF-16 code units, not user-perceived characters. [...s] iterates code points, but grapheme clusters may still span several code points. Strings are immutable and numbers are IEEE-754 doubles, exact only through Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER.

prompts.prompt: Why does `console.log('A'); setTimeout(()=>log('D')); Promise.resolve().then(()=>log('C')); log('B')` print A B C D?
prompts.answer: Run the current job to completion (A, B), then drain all microtasks (promise handlers, queueMicrotask, await continuations) -> C, then the next macrotask (timer) -> D. await always yields, resuming after it in a microtask even for a non-promise.

prompts.prompt: For Promise.all, allSettled, race, and any: what does each fulfill with and when does each reject?
prompts.answer: all: fulfills with all values in input order, rejects on first rejection. allSettled: fulfills with outcome records, never rejects. race: settles with the first settlement (rejects if that is a rejection). any: fulfills with the first fulfillment, rejects with an AggregateError only if all reject.

prompts.prompt: How do you cancel a fetch with both a manual trigger and a timeout, and why is a promise itself not cancellable?
prompts.answer: Create an AbortController and pass a combined signal via AbortSignal.any([ctrl.signal, AbortSignal.timeout(5000)]) into fetch; call ctrl.abort() to cancel. Cancellation is cooperative: a promise itself is not cancellable, so the underlying operation must observe the signal, which must be threaded through every layer.

prompts.prompt: Why does fetch not throw on a 404, and why does forEach(async ...) finish early?
prompts.answer: fetch rejects only on network or abort errors, not HTTP 4xx/5xx, so you must check response.ok. forEach ignores returned promises and does not await callbacks, so it finishes without waiting; use for...of or Promise.all instead.

prompts.prompt: Describe the debounce template and how flush/cancel extend it.
prompts.answer: Hold a timer id in closure; on each call clearTimeout(timer) then timer = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(this, args), ms) so the trailing edge fires only after silence. Expose cancel = () => clearTimeout(timer); flush stores the pending args/receiver, clears the timer, and invokes fn immediately.

prompts.prompt: Describe leading-edge throttle and how you add a trailing call.
prompts.answer: Leading: keep a ready flag; if not ready return, else set ready=false, call fn.apply(this,args), and setTimeout to reset ready after ms. Trailing: while not ready, save the latest [this,args] as pending; when the timer resets ready, if pending exists re-invoke with those saved args so the latest call wins.

prompts.prompt: Describe the memoize template and the pitfalls of its default JSON key.
prompts.answer: Keep a Map cache; compute key k = key(...args) (default JSON.stringify(args)); if !cache.has(k) set cache.set(k, fn.apply(this,args)); return cache.get(k). JSON keys fail on cycles, key-order differences, functions, and identity-sensitive objects; also decide whether to cache thrown errors/rejections or allow retry.

prompts.prompt: Describe the curry template using fn.length, and what is the caveat with fn.length?
prompts.answer: curried(...a) returns fn.apply(this,a) when a.length >= fn.length, otherwise returns (...b) => curried(...a, ...b) to accumulate arguments. Caveat: fn.length ignores rest parameters and stops at the first default parameter, so an explicit arity is more robust.

prompts.prompt: How do you implement Promise.all from scratch, preserving order and the empty case?
prompts.answer: Return a new Promise; if the input is empty resolve([]) immediately; keep an out array and a left counter; for each item, Promise.resolve(x).then(v => { out[i]=v; if (--left===0) resolve(out); }, reject). Writing out[i] preserves input order (not finish order), and passing reject makes the first rejection win.

prompts.prompt: How are allSettled and any built by adapting Promise.all's approach?
prompts.answer: allSettled: map each input to Promise.resolve(x).then(value => ({status:'fulfilled', value}), reason => ({status:'rejected', reason})) then Promise.all them, so it never rejects. any inverts all: resolve on the first fulfillment, collect rejections in an errs array, and reject with new AggregateError(errs) only when left reaches 0.

prompts.prompt: Describe a concurrency-limited mapLimit and why the shared index is safe.
prompts.answer: Create out array and a shared next=0; spawn Math.min(limit, xs.length) worker() functions, each looping i = next++ and if i < xs.length doing out[i] = await fn(xs[i], i) until exhausted; await Promise.all of the workers. The index is safe because JS is single-threaded, so next++ cannot interleave.

prompts.prompt: Describe the retry-with-backoff template and its policy rules.
prompts.answer: Loop up to `tries`; call signal?.throwIfAborted() then return await fn(); on catch, if the error is not transient or it's the last attempt, break and rethrow the original error, else wait delay = base * 2**i + Math.random()*base (exponential backoff plus jitter). Retry only transient failures on idempotent operations, bound attempts, honor Retry-After, and never stack retries across layers.

prompts.prompt: In an event emitter's emit, why iterate over a snapshot of listeners, and what does on() return?
prompts.answer: emit iterates [...(map.get(type) ?? [])], a snapshot, so adding/removing listeners during dispatch has defined behavior (mutation-safe). on(type, fn) adds fn to the type's Set and returns an unsubscribe function that calls off(type, fn); once wraps a listener that unsubscribes itself before calling fn.

prompts.prompt: Outline the deepEqual algorithm for plain objects/arrays and how it handles cycles.
prompts.answer: Identity via Object.is short-circuits true; guard non-objects/null as false; use a seen Map keyed by a to detect cycle pairs (seen.get(a) === b -> true) before recursing; require matching Array.isArray, equal key counts, and that every own key of a exists on b (Object.hasOwn) with deepEqual values. It's scoped to plain objects/arrays; extend by tag for Date/Map/Set before the key walk.

prompts.prompt: Describe groupBy and a safe get(o, path, def) that supports 'a.b[0]' paths.
prompts.answer: groupBy(xs, keyFn): for each x compute k=keyFn(x) and push x into a Map bucket created on first use, returning the Map. get: parse the path (array, or string via match(/[^.[\]]+/g)) into parts, walk cur=o[k] and return def if cur == null mid-walk or the final value is undefined.

prompts.prompt: Name the three phases of a React update in order, and say what each is responsible for.
prompts.answer: Render (compute JSX purely from a snapshot of props/state, no side effects), Commit (apply DOM changes and set refs), then Effects run afterward; layout effects run synchronously after DOM mutation but before paint.

prompts.prompt: A handler reads count, calls setCount several times based on the current value, and only one increment sticks. What is the bug and the fix?
prompts.answer: The handler sees a stale render snapshot of count, so each setter uses the same value. Use functional updates like setCount(c => c + 1) so each queued update builds on the previous.

prompts.prompt: How does React decide whether to preserve or reset a component's state across renders, and how do you deliberately reset a subtree?
prompts.answer: React preserves state by component type plus position in the rendered tree; changing a component's key intentionally resets that subtree. Defining a component function inside another component creates a new type each render and can also reset state.

prompts.prompt: When is using the array index as a list key unsafe, and what makes a good key?
prompts.answer: Index is unsafe when items can be inserted, deleted, or reordered because state binds to the wrong row. A good key is stable among siblings and represents the entity, with IDs generated when data is created, not during render.

prompts.prompt: State the effect contract: what do setup and cleanup represent, how often can they run, and what does Strict Mode expose?
prompts.answer: An effect starts synchronization with an external system and its cleanup stops it; it may start and stop many times, not only on mount/unmount. Strict Mode in development runs an extra setup/cleanup cycle, so synchronization must be idempotent.

prompts.prompt: An effect that fetches by id keeps firing in a loop and a late response can overwrite newer data. Outline the correct effect.
prompts.answer: Create an AbortController inside the effect, pass its signal to the fetch, ignore AbortError in the rejection handler, and return () => ctrl.abort() as cleanup, with [id] as the dependency so changing id cancels the stale request. Put every reactive value read in the deps instead of silencing the linter.

prompts.prompt: Contrast useRef and state: when does each trigger a render, and what is each for?
prompts.answer: Mutating a ref's .current does not cause a render and holds things like DOM nodes, timers, or the latest handle (an escape hatch); a state setter schedules a render and is the declarative source of truth for anything visible in the UI. Don't read/write refs during render except for predictable initialization.

prompts.prompt: Distinguish memo, useMemo, and useCallback, and name the single thing that defeats all of them.
prompts.answer: memo skips a component's render when props compare equal, useMemo caches a computed value, and useCallback caches a function's identity; a single always-new object or function passed as a prop or dependency defeats the memoization.

prompts.prompt: Why does a Context provider cause render storms, and what are the fixes named in the guide?
prompts.answer: Every consumer rerenders when the provider's value identity changes. Fix by memoizing the value only when its dependencies are stable, splitting contexts by update frequency/responsibility, and for high-frequency external state subscribe with selectors via useSyncExternalStore.

prompts.prompt: What does a portal change and not change, and what problem is it good for?
prompts.answer: A portal changes only DOM placement, not React ownership or event propagation, which still follow the React tree. It is useful for modals/popovers that must escape parent clipping or stacking contexts.

prompts.prompt: Distinguish controlled vs uncontrolled inputs, and name the classic silent form-submit bug.
prompts.answer: Controlled means React state is the source of truth via value/onChange; uncontrolled means the DOM holds the value via defaultValue/ref, and you must not switch mid-lifecycle. The classic bug is forgetting e.preventDefault() in the submit handler, causing a full-page form post.

prompts.prompt: What does a Suspense boundary own versus an error boundary, and where should you place them?
prompts.answer: A Suspense boundary owns the pending fallback for Suspense-integrated code/data (including lazy-loaded components), while an error boundary catches render and async-action errors. Place both around the smallest meaningful UX region rather than replacing the whole page for one slow or failing panel.

prompts.prompt: State the CSS cascade resolution order from highest priority to lowest.
prompts.answer: Origin/importance, then cascade layer, then specificity, then scope proximity, then source order; specificity only compares among rules still competing.

prompts.prompt: Give the specificity ordering of selector types, and what :where() contributes.
prompts.answer: IDs beat classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, which beat elements/pseudo-elements; :where() adds zero specificity so it keeps component selectors low and overridable.

prompts.prompt: What does the box model include, and what does box-sizing: border-box change?
prompts.answer: By default an element's rendered box size is content plus padding plus border; box-sizing: border-box makes the declared width/height include padding and border. Note vertical margins can collapse in normal block flow.

prompts.prompt: A modal cannot appear above a sibling even with a huge z-index. Explain why raising z-index fails and what to check.
prompts.answer: z-index only compares within the same stacking context, and properties like transform, opacity, isolation, or a positioned z-index on an ancestor create new contexts that trap the element. Inspect the stacking-context ancestry and portal the modal to the top layer/root instead of increasing z-index.

prompts.prompt: When should you reach for flexbox versus grid, and what do auto-fit and auto-fill differ on?
prompts.answer: Flexbox lays out one axis (main axis from flex-direction, justify-content on main, align-items on cross); grid places items in two dimensions. In grid repeat(), auto-fit collapses empty tracks while auto-fill preserves them.

prompts.prompt: Text truncation with ellipsis on a flex child is not working. What is the recipe and the common blocker?
prompts.answer: Use min-width:0 on the flex child (its intrinsic minimum size blocks shrink by default) plus overflow:hidden; text-overflow:ellipsis; white-space:nowrap on the text; multi-line requires a line-clamp decision.

prompts.prompt: What does each positioning value resolve against: absolute, fixed, and sticky?
prompts.answer: absolute positions against the nearest positioned containing block, fixed usually against the viewport, and sticky needs a scroll container plus an inset value to work.

prompts.prompt: Contrast a media query with a container query, and give the fluid-first responsive rule for adding breakpoints.
prompts.answer: A media query responds to the viewport or user preference while a container query responds to a component's available space (via container-type). Start fluid with clamp/min/max, wrapping, and flexible tracks, and add a breakpoint only where the content actually fails, not for a named device.

prompts.prompt: What does the FRANK mnemonic stand for, and what is each letter's one-line concern?
prompts.answer: Focus (visible ring; moved into modals/restored/sent to new heading), Role (correct semantic element with state attrs that update), Announce (live regions for anything that changes without reload), Name (every control has an accessible name), Keyboard (reach and operate everything with keys alone).

prompts.prompt: Give the precedence order for computing an accessible name among aria-labelledby, aria-label, visible text, and title/placeholder.
prompts.answer: aria-labelledby (pointer to visible element ids) wins over everything, then aria-label (a raw string, silently overrides visible text), then the element's visible text, then title/placeholder as a last resort. Mnemonic: a pointer beats a string beats the text beats a placeholder.

prompts.prompt: For a hand-rolled role="button" on a div, which two keys must you handle, and what extra call is required and why?
prompts.answer: Handle both Enter and Space; call preventDefault on Space so the page doesn't scroll. Native <button> does all of this for free.

prompts.prompt: For streaming chat/assistant replies, should the live region be polite or assertive, and which role plus attribute announces only new tokens rather than the whole growing message?
prompts.answer: Always polite (assertive on every token is torture) — a streaming reply is always polite. Use role="log" with aria-relevant="additions" so only newly added text is announced, not the entire message.

prompts.prompt: Map the three live-region roles alert, status, and log to their implicit live/atomic semantics and typical use.
prompts.answer: alert = assertive + atomic (errors), status = polite + atomic ("saved"/toasts), log = polite + non-atomic (chat message list). Mnemonic: alert screams, status states, log logs.

prompts.prompt: What is the "trigger trio" — the three attributes any show/hide control carries — and what does each do?
prompts.answer: aria-expanded (true/false on the trigger, is the controlled thing open), aria-controls (id of the panel/menu/listbox it toggles), and aria-haspopup (menu/listbox/dialog, only if it opens a real popup). All three go together on any disclosure control.

prompts.prompt: Describe the focus-management contract for a modal dialog: on open, while open, and on close, plus the required role attribute.
prompts.answer: On open, move focus into the dialog (first field or the dialog itself); while open, trap Tab/Shift+Tab to cycle within; Esc closes; on close, restore focus to the trigger. The dialog carries aria-modal="true" (native <dialog>.showModal() gives the trap, Esc, and inert backdrop free).

prompts.prompt: On a route/page change in an SPA, where should focus be sent, and what tabindex trick makes that target focusable?
prompts.answer: Send focus to the new page's <h1> heading. Give the heading tabindex="-1" so it is focusable by script but skipped by Tab.

prompts.prompt: Contrast roving tabindex ("Move") vs aria-activedescendant ("Mark"): where does DOM focus live in each, and which pattern fits a combobox vs a toolbar/menu/tabs?
prompts.answer: Move/roving tabindex: real DOM focus moves item-to-item (exactly one item tabindex=0, rest -1) — use for toolbar/menu/tabs/radio group/tree. Mark/aria-activedescendant: focus stays on the container (tabindex=0) and you point aria-activedescendant at the active child — use for combobox/grid where focus must stay in the input.

prompts.prompt: Implement roving tabindex for an arrow-navigable list: what tabindex values do items carry, and what happens on ArrowDown/Up/Home/End?
prompts.answer: Exactly one item is tabindex=0 and all others tabindex=-1, keeping the widget a single Tab stop. On arrow, update which index is active, preventDefault, then call .focus() on the new item: ArrowDown/Up move next/prev (wrapping), Home goes to first, End to last.

prompts.prompt: Give the keyboard contract for a menu button: what opens it (and where does focus land), how do you move between items, what does typing a letter do, and what does Esc do?
prompts.answer: Enter/Space/Down open and focus the first item (Up on the button opens and focuses the last item); Up/Down move between items; a-z does typeahead to the matching item; Esc closes and returns focus to the button; Tab closes and moves on.

prompts.prompt: Give the keyboard contract for a tablist: how do you get in/out with Tab, which keys switch tabs, and which keys activate in manual mode?
prompts.answer: Tab moves into the tablist (landing on the active tab) then out to the panel; Left/Right arrows move prev/next tab via roving (Home/End jump to first/last); Enter or Space activate the tab in manual-activation mode.

prompts.prompt: Give the keyboard contract for a combobox/listbox and name which focus pattern keeps the caret in the input while arrowing options.
prompts.answer: Down/Up open and move through options, Alt+Down opens without moving, Enter commits the highlighted option, Esc closes/clears; typing filters. Focus stays in the input via aria-activedescendant (Mark), which points at the highlighted option.

prompts.prompt: Name the six landmark roles and their native HTML equivalents, and how you distinguish two navigations.
prompts.answer: banner=<header>, navigation=<nav>, main=<main> (one per page), complementary=<aside>, contentinfo=<footer>, region=named <section>. Two navs are distinguished with aria-label (e.g. "Primary" vs "Footer").

prompts.prompt: Which ARIA attribute carries the state for each of: checkbox/switch, toggle button, tab/option selection, and the "you are here" nav item?
prompts.answer: aria-checked (true/false/mixed) for checkbox/radio/switch, aria-pressed (true/false/mixed) for a toggle button, aria-selected for option/tab/row selection, and aria-current (page for a nav link) for the "you are here" item. Check-like things get checked; buttons get pressed.

prompts.prompt: What is the live-region "gotcha" about DOM timing, and how do you avoid it?
prompts.answer: The live region must already exist in the DOM before you inject text, or nothing is announced. Render an empty <div aria-live="polite"> on mount, then fill it later — never create the region with its text at the same time.

prompts.prompt: Explain the difference between the native disabled attribute and aria-disabled, and the visible-focus rule for custom controls.
prompts.answer: Native disabled removes the control from tab order (undiscoverable), while aria-disabled keeps it focusable so users find it and learn why it's off. Never use outline:none without a :focus-visible replacement — every control needs a visible focus ring.

prompts.prompt: Recite the 35-45 minute coding solve loop in order, from the opening minutes to after you have a correct solution.
prompts.answer: 0-4: restate I/O, examples, constraints, mutation, duplicates, ordering, edge cases. 4-8: name brute force and its bottleneck, propose a pattern, justify it from input structure. 8-12: define the invariant/data structure and complexity before coding. 12-28: code in narrated chunks with boring control flow. 28-35: dry-run normal + edge, fixing from the invariant. 35+: optimize or discuss alternatives only after correct.

prompts.prompt: For each recognition cue, name the pattern to reach for: (a) contiguous longest/shortest, (b) subarray sum / range query, (c) next greater / nesting, (d) monotonic yes/no answer, (e) k best / cheapest frontier, (f) prerequisites, (g) all combinations.
prompts.answer: (a) sliding window; (b) prefix sum; (c) stack / monotonic stack; (d) binary search; (e) heap; (f) topological sort; (g) backtracking.

prompts.prompt: When do you reach for a hash map vs a set, and what time/space do you quote?
prompts.answer: Reach for a hash structure when you need O(1) expected membership, complement, frequency, canonical grouping, dedupe, or last-seen position; Map when the value matters, Set for membership. Quote O(n) expected time and O(k) distinct-state space.

prompts.prompt: Recite the prefix-sum + hash-map template for counting subarrays that sum to K, and explain why the count map is seeded with {0: 1}.
prompts.answer: Walk the array keeping a running sum; at each element add count.get(sum - k) to the answer, then increment count.get(sum). Seed {0:1} so a subarray starting at index 0 (whose prefix equals k) is counted. O(n) time and space. Invariant: before processing a[i] the map summarizes exactly the earlier prefixes.

prompts.prompt: Prefix-sum variants: how do you handle (a) longest subarray with equal 0/1 counts, and (b) subarray sum divisible by K in JavaScript?
prompts.answer: (a) Map each 0 to a -1 contribution and look for two prefixes with the same value (difference 0). (b) Group by equal prefix remainders, normalizing negatives since JS % keeps the dividend's sign: ((x % k) + k) % k.

prompts.prompt: Name the three two-pointer shapes and the key idea of the converging-on-sorted variant.
prompts.answer: Converging on sorted data (the comparison tells which side cannot participate, so discard it: if sum<target l++, else r--), reader/writer (scan with fast, write kept values at slow), and same-direction-with-gap (kth-from-end, cycle/middle, merge streams). Converging is O(n) after any sort.

prompts.prompt: Recite the variable-length sliding window skeleton and the rule difference between 'longest valid' and 'shortest valid'.
prompts.answer: For each r: add(a[r]); while (!valid()) remove(a[l++]); update best. O(n) with O(1)-updatable state (count map, sum, distinct/max-freq). Longest valid: shrink while invalid, record after shrinking. Shortest valid: shrink while valid, recording before each removal. Trigger: contiguous longest/shortest with a constraint.

prompts.prompt: Describe the fixed-window / monotonic-deque template for sliding-window maximum and its complexity.
prompts.answer: For fixed k, add the right element and drop index r-k, recording once the window is full. For sliding max keep a deque of indices with decreasing values: pop dominated indices from the back while a[back] <= a[r], push r, shift an expired front (index <= r-k), record a[front] when r >= k-1. Each index enters/leaves once, so O(n).

prompts.prompt: Recite the monotonic-stack 'next greater element' template and state what the stack holds.
prompts.answer: Iterate indices; while the stack is non-empty and a[i] > a[top], pop j and set ans[j] = i; then push i. The stack holds indices whose next-greater answer is still unknown, values decreasing; the current value resolves all dominated entries. O(n), each index pushed/popped once.

prompts.prompt: Contrast the exact binary-search template with the lower-bound template (loop condition, interval, mid branch, return), and give upper bound.
prompts.answer: Exact: inclusive [l,r] with while (l<=r); if a[m]<x set l=m+1 else r=m-1; return m or -1. Lower bound: half-open [l,r) with while (l<r); if a[m]>=x set r=m else l=m+1; return l = first index with a[i]>=x. Upper bound uses a[m]>x; frequency of x = upper - lower. Never mix inclusive and half-open templates.

prompts.prompt: What is 'binary search on the answer', what phrasing triggers it, why must the predicate be monotonic, and what is its complexity?
prompts.answer: Search for the minimum X such that feasible(X), where feasibility is monotonic (false...false, true...true); pick bounds containing an answer and binary-search the first feasible X. It's valid only because the predicate never flips back; complexity O(log range x feasibility cost). Trigger: 'min/max X such that feasible(X)', e.g. Koko min eating speed.

prompts.prompt: Heaps: which heap for k-largest vs k-smallest (with complexity), and what structures give running median and merge-of-k-sorted?
prompts.answer: K largest -> min-heap of size k, evict the smallest; K smallest -> max-heap of size k; O(n log k) time, O(k) space, final heap not globally sorted. Running median = max-heap low half + min-heap high half (O(log n) insert, O(1) query). Merge k sorted = heap of one frontier item per source, O(N log k).

prompts.prompt: For merging vs. max-non-overlap interval problems, what do you sort by, and recite the merge sweep rule?
prompts.answer: Merge/insert: sort by start. Max non-overlap / min removals: sort by end. Merge rule: after sorting by start, for each [s,e], if s <= last[1] extend last[1] = max(last[1], e), else push a new interval. O(n log n). Clarify closed vs half-open and whether touching endpoints overlap.

prompts.prompt: Cycle detection: how do you find a linked-list cycle and its entry (Floyd), and how do DFS colors detect a directed-graph cycle?
prompts.answer: Floyd: advance slow one step and fast two; slow===fast means a cycle, then move one pointer to head and advance both one step until equal to find the entry (compare identity). Directed graph: color white/gray/black; a gray node on the current recursion path is a back edge = cycle. A plain visited set is insufficient because black nodes are safe to revisit.

prompts.prompt: DFS vs BFS: what is each best for, when do you mark a node visited, and what is traversal complexity?
prompts.answer: DFS for reachability, components, and backtracking (stack/recursion, may go deep); BFS for fewest unweighted edges and levels (queue, frontier may be wide). Mark visited when enqueuing (BFS) or before recursing (DFS), never on dequeue. Traversal is O(V+E); a grid is O(RC), not O(R+C).

prompts.prompt: Recite the backtracking pattern for subsets/combinations, including where copies happen and why a start index is used. What is the cost of generating permutations?
prompts.answer: Pattern: choose -> recurse -> unchoose on one shared path; record by pushing a copy [...path]. dfs(start) records the path, loops i from start, pushes a[i], recurses dfs(i+1), pops; the start index prevents different orderings of the same combination. Permutations cost O(n * n!) including output copying, since output size is already exponential.

prompts.prompt: Recite the DP five-step ritual you state before coding, and note the coin/knapsack loop-order rule.
prompts.answer: 1. State: one sentence for the dp indices/flags. 2. Transition: choices and smaller states used. 3. Base: smallest valid/empty states. 4. Order: dependencies computed first. 5. Answer: which state/aggregate is returned. Loop order matters: unbounded combinations use coins outer + amount ascending, order-sensitive counts use amount outer, 0/1 uses amount descending.

prompts.prompt: Which two CSS properties should you default to animating, and why are they cheap?
prompts.answer: Animate transform and opacity. They only trigger the Composite stage and run on the GPU/compositor thread, off the main thread, so they stay smooth even while JS is busy.

prompts.prompt: Name the four stages of the browser's pixel/rendering pipeline in order, and give an example property that triggers each of the costly ones.
prompts.answer: Style, Layout, Paint, Composite. Layout (reflow, worst cost) is triggered by width/height/top/left/margin/padding; Paint (bad) by color/background/box-shadow/border-radius; Composite (cheap, GPU) by transform/opacity/filter.

prompts.prompt: Why is animating width to fill a progress bar worse for performance than using transform: scaleX, and what's the tradeoff of scaleX?
prompts.answer: width triggers Layout (reflow) each frame while scaleX is composite-only, so scaleX is the perf answer. The tradeoff is that scaleX distorts children (text/icons stretch), so use width when the bar has content.

prompts.prompt: What does will-change: transform do, and what's the hygiene rule around it?
prompts.answer: It promotes the element to its own compositor layer. Use it sparingly and remove it after the animation, because each layer costs memory.

prompts.prompt: When should you reach for @keyframes + animation instead of a CSS transition?
prompts.answer: Use @keyframes/animation when there's no state change to trigger a transition, i.e. looping or multistep motion like spinners, skeletons, indeterminate bars, and blinking carets. A transition needs two interpolatable endpoints triggered by a value change (hover, class toggle, state).

prompts.prompt: For JS-driven motion, which API should you use and which must you avoid? Also state the easing rule of thumb for enter vs exit.
prompts.answer: Use requestAnimationFrame, never setInterval. Rule of thumb: ease-out on the way in (fast to slow, snappy), ease-in on the way out (slow to fast, gets out of the way).

prompts.prompt: A React exit animation never plays. What's the cause and how do you fix it?
prompts.answer: Setting state unmounts the element instantly, so the exit transition never plays because the node is already gone. Keep it mounted with an 'out' class until the transition ends, then remove it on onTransitionEnd (or use AnimatePresence / react-transition-group).

prompts.prompt: How do you honor prefers-reduced-motion in a motion component, and why does it matter?
prompts.answer: In an @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) block, set animation-duration and transition-duration to ~0.01ms !important, animation-iteration-count to 1, and scroll-behavior to auto. It kills non-essential motion for vestibular users while the component still works, a definition-of-done a11y item.

prompts.prompt: Why should you avoid transition: all and animating box-shadow, and what do you do instead for the shadow?
prompts.answer: transition: all animates properties you didn't mean to, causing layout jank and surprise transitions, so list properties explicitly. box-shadow is paint-heavy, so instead animate the opacity of a pseudo-element that holds the shadow.

prompts.prompt: In the 45-minute interview loop, name the six phases in order with their rough time budgets.
prompts.answer: Frame (0-5), Quantify (5-10), Contract (10-15), Baseline end-to-end (15-28), Deep dive on the top two risks (28-40), Close with cuts/degraded mode/rollout (40-45).

prompts.prompt: Give the four-line back-of-envelope capacity model (the equations), including which law gives concurrency.
prompts.answer: avg_qps = active_users x actions_per_user / 86,400; peak_qps = avg_qps x peak_factor; storage/day = writes_per_day x bytes_per_item x replication; concurrency = arrival_rate x time_in_system (Little's Law).

prompts.prompt: For a safe retry of an unsafe write, what should the idempotency key be bound to and what must be stored?
prompts.answer: Bind the key to caller + operation + payload hash and store the terminal response with a retention window, so a replayed request returns the stored result instead of re-running the side effect.

prompts.prompt: For cursor pagination, what should the cursor be built over and what tuple is commonly used?
prompts.answer: Build the cursor over a stable total order, commonly (created_at, id), encoded as an opaque token, and define whether it has snapshot or live semantics.

prompts.prompt: A rate-limit spec needs which four things, plus what response on rejection?
prompts.answer: Scope (user/tenant/IP/token cost), algorithm, burst size, and a 429 with Retry-After; page size and query cost should be bounded too.

prompts.prompt: Contrast cache-aside and write-through: who loads on miss, and what does each trade on freshness vs latency?
prompts.answer: Cache-aside: the app loads on miss, so it survives cache loss but the first miss is slow and you own stale invalidation. Write-through: the write path updates the cache, giving fresher reads at the cost of higher write latency and dual-write care.

prompts.prompt: For a composite B-tree index, in what order do the columns go, and which index type serves approximate vector search?
prompts.answer: Put equality columns first, then range/sort columns (verify leftmost-prefix behavior); HNSW/IVF indexes serve approximate vector search.

prompts.prompt: How do you pick a shard key, and what do hash vs range vs directory partitioning each trade? Does consistent hashing fix a hot key?
prompts.answer: Pick the shard key from access patterns and distribution so common queries hit one shard and hot entities don't share a partition; hash gives even point access but poor ranges, range gives efficient scans but a hot tail, directory gives flexible placement but a metadata-service dependency, and consistent hashing reduces data movement but does not solve a single hot key.

prompts.prompt: How does the transactional outbox avoid the dual-write problem when publishing events?
prompts.answer: Write the business state and an outbox row in one local transaction, have a separate relay read the outbox and publish to the broker, and let consumers dedupe, so nothing is lost if the process crashes between the two systems.

prompts.prompt: Name four ways to give a reader read-your-writes consistency against lagging replicas.
prompts.answer: Pin the author to the primary briefly, carry a write timestamp/LSN token, read from a write-through cache, or wait until the replica catches up.

prompts.prompt: Describe the hybrid feed fanout strategy and what sets the push/pull threshold.
prompts.answer: Push (write to recipient inboxes) for normal producers and pull (fetch-and-merge on read) for high-fanout/celebrity producers, merging and ranking on read; the follower distribution and read:write ratio set the threshold.

prompts.prompt: On WebSocket reconnect, how does a client recover missed messages, and which state may be dropped under pressure?
prompts.answer: The client sends its last cursor/sequence and the server replays from a durable log/store then resumes live delivery; ephemeral presence/typing/read-receipt state is lossy TTL state and may be dropped.

prompts.prompt: Size the read/write QPS and storage for a URL shortener (create + redirect), stating your assumptions.
prompts.answer:
Assume: 10M new links/day, 100:1 read:write, ~500 B/record, 5-yr retention.
Writes: 10M ÷ 100k s ≈ 100/s (×5 peak ≈ 500)
Reads: 100× writes = 1B redirects/day ÷ 100k ≈ 10k reads/s
Storage: 10M × 500 B = 5 GB/day; ×365 ≈ 1.8 TB/yr (×3 replication ≈ 5.5 TB/yr)
Headline: ~10k read QPS, ~100 write QPS; storage is trivial (single-digit TB/yr) — this is a read-cache problem, not a storage one.

prompts.prompt: Size the read/write QPS and storage for a Twitter-style timeline (post tweet + read home timeline), stating your assumptions.
prompts.answer:
Assume: 200M DAU, 0.5 tweets/user/day (100M/day), 50 timeline reads/user/day, ~300 B/tweet, ~200 followers avg.
Writes: 100M ÷ 100k ≈ 1k/s (×5 peak ≈ 5k)
Reads: 200M × 50 = 10B/day ÷ 100k ≈ 100k reads/s
Fanout: 100M × 200 = 20B inbox writes/day ÷ 100k ≈ 200k/s
Storage: 100M × 300 B = 30 GB/day ×3 ≈ 90 GB/day tweets (~33 TB/yr); fanout inboxes dwarf this.
Headline: ~100k read QPS, but the ~200k/s write-fanout is the real cost driver — hence hybrid fanout.

prompts.prompt: Size the read/write QPS and storage for a group-chat/messaging system (send + deliver messages), stating your assumptions.
prompts.answer:
Assume: 500M DAU, 40 msgs sent/user/day, ~3 recipients/msg, ~100 B/msg, 1-yr retention.
Writes: 500M × 40 = 20B/day ÷ 100k ≈ 200k writes/s (×5 peak ≈ 1M)
Reads: deliveries = 20B × 3 = 60B/day ÷ 100k ≈ 600k reads/s
Storage: 20B × 100 B = 2 TB/day ×3 ≈ 6 TB/day (~2 PB/yr)
Headline: ~200k msg writes/s (1M peak), multi-PB/yr — partition by conversation, keep durable msgs separate from ephemeral presence.

prompts.prompt: Size the read/write QPS and storage for a read-time (pull) news feed that merges and ranks friends' posts, stating your assumptions.
prompts.answer:
Assume: 300M DAU, 30 feed opens/user/day, ~300 friends merged+ranked per open, 0.5 posts/user/day, ~2 KB/response.
Writes: 300M × 0.5 = 150M posts/day ÷ 100k ≈ 1.5k/s
Reads: 300M × 30 = 9B opens/day ÷ 100k ≈ 90k feed QPS (×5 peak ≈ 450k)
Amplification: 90k × 300 candidate fetches → forces cache/precompute or fanout-on-write.
Storage: 150M × 1 KB = 150 GB/day ×3 ≈ 450 GB/day (~55 TB/yr posts).
Headline: ~90k feed reads/s with 300× read-time fanout — the trigger to switch to hybrid fanout.

prompts.prompt: Size the read/write QPS and storage for an Instagram-style photo-sharing service (upload + view), stating your assumptions.
prompts.answer:
Assume: 500M DAU, 0.2 uploads/user/day (100M/day), 20 views/user/day, ~2 MB/photo incl thumbnails.
Writes: 100M ÷ 100k ≈ 1k uploads/s (×5 peak ≈ 5k)
Reads: 500M × 20 = 10B views/day ÷ 100k ≈ 100k views/s (CDN-served)
Storage: 100M × 2 MB = 200 TB/day ×3 ≈ 600 TB/day (~220 PB/yr)
Headline: ~100k image reads/s off the CDN; ~200 TB/day of new blobs to object storage — metadata QPS is small, bytes dominate.

prompts.prompt: Size the read/write QPS and storage for a YouTube-style video platform (upload + view), stating your assumptions.
prompts.answer:
Assume: 500M DAU, 5 views/user/day, 500k uploads/day, ~1 GB/video after multi-rendition transcode.
Writes: 500k uploads ÷ 100k ≈ 5/s (×5 peak ≈ 25)
Reads: 500M × 5 = 2.5B view-starts/day ÷ 100k ≈ 25k starts/s
Storage: 500k × 1 GB = 500 TB/day ×3 ≈ 1.5 PB/day (~550 PB/yr)
Headline: ~25k view-starts/s and ~500 TB/day new video — CDN egress bandwidth, not origin QPS, is the constraint.

prompts.prompt: Size the read/write QPS and storage for a notification fanout system (event in, per-recipient delivery out), stating your assumptions.
prompts.answer:
Assume: 200M DAU, 5 triggering events/user/day (1B/day), ~100 recipients/event, ~200 B/notification, 30-day retention.
Ingest: 1B ÷ 100k ≈ 10k events/s (×5 peak ≈ 50k)
Deliveries: 1B × 100 = 100B/day ÷ 100k ≈ 1M/s (×5 peak ≈ 5M)
Storage: 100B × 200 B = 20 TB/day ×3 ≈ 60 TB/day; ×30 ≈ 1.8 PB retained
Headline: ~1M deliveries/s avg (5M peak) — fanout amplification and celebrity producers are the design, not the 10k ingest.

prompts.prompt: Size the read/write QPS and storage for a typeahead/autocomplete service (per-keystroke prefix queries), stating your assumptions.
prompts.answer:
Assume: 100M DAU, 20 searches/user/day, ~5 keystroke-queries/search, ~50 B/response, trie rebuilt offline daily.
Reads: 100M × 20 × 5 = 10B prefix-queries/day ÷ 100k ≈ 100k QPS (×5 peak ≈ 500k)
Writes: none online — top-N prefixes rebuilt from query logs in batch.
Storage: ~100M prefixes × ~100 B ≈ 10 GB trie, in-memory, ×3 replicas ≈ 30 GB.
Headline: ~100k prefix QPS (500k peak) against an in-memory read-only trie; all writes are offline batch — latency, not storage, is the bar.

prompts.prompt: Size the read/write QPS and storage for a distributed rate-limiter counter store (one check per API request), stating your assumptions.
prompts.answer:
Assume: 50k API req/s baseline (×5 peak 250k), 1 atomic counter op per request, per-(user,route) sliding window, TTL keys.
Ops: 1 INCR/request → 50k ops/s (×5 peak ≈ 250k); each op reads+increments one counter atomically (read ≈ write).
Storage: ~10M users × a few routes ≈ 50M live keys × ~100 B ≈ 5 GB in Redis, expired each window.
Headline: ~50k INCR/s (250k peak), memory-bound at ~5 GB of hot keys with near-zero durable storage — size RAM and hot-key spread, not disk.

prompts.prompt: Size the read/write QPS and storage for ride-sharing driver location updates (GPS ping ingest + nearby query), stating your assumptions.
prompts.answer:
Assume: 2M active drivers ping every 4 s, 5M active riders query nearby every 5 s, ~100 B/ping, latest-only hot state.
Writes: 2M ÷ 4 s = 500k location writes/s (×2 surge ≈ 1M)
Reads: 5M ÷ 5 s = 1M nearby-queries/s
Storage: latest-only 2M × 100 B ≈ 200 MB in-memory geo index (geohash/S2); trip history archived async.
Headline: ~500k writes/s + ~1M geo-queries/s against an in-memory geospatial index that keeps only latest-wins position — durable ping history is optional.

prompts.prompt: Size the read/write QPS and storage for e-commerce checkout (catalog browse + order commit), stating your assumptions.
prompts.answer:
Assume: 50M DAU, 0.1 orders/user/day (5M/day), ~50 catalog views per order, ~2 KB/order+line-items, 7-yr retention.
Writes: 5M orders ÷ 100k ≈ 50/s (×5 peak ≈ 250; ×10 flash-sale ≈ 500)
Reads: 50M × 50 = 2.5B catalog views/day ÷ 100k ≈ 25k reads/s (cache-served)
Storage: 5M × 2 KB = 10 GB/day ×3 ≈ 30 GB/day (~11 TB/yr; ~80 TB over 7 yr)
Headline: only low-hundreds order writes/s — but each must be transactional/idempotent; ~25k catalog reads/s served from cache.

prompts.prompt: Size the write throughput and storage for a distributed logging/metrics ingestion pipeline, stating your assumptions.
prompts.answer:
Assume: 10k hosts, each ~1k log lines/s + 200 metrics per 10 s, ~300 B/line, ~10:1 compression, 30-day hot retention.
Log writes: 10k × 1k = 10M events/s (batched)
Metric writes: 10k × 200 ÷ 10 = 200k datapoints/s
Storage: 10M/s × 300 B = 3 GB/s ≈ 260 TB/day raw → ~26 TB/day compressed; ×30 ≈ 780 TB hot
Headline: ~10M log events/s ingest and ~26 TB/day compressed — batch, compress, and tier aggressively; sample non-critical streams before they dominate cost.

prompts.prompt: Size the concurrency, token volume, and rough cost for a ChatGPT-like assistant (streamed chat), stating your assumptions.
prompts.answer:
Assume: 10M DAU, 10 msgs/user/day (100M/day), ~1k input + 500 output tokens/msg, ~10 s avg stream; assume $1/1M input, $4/1M output.
Requests: 100M ÷ 100k ≈ 1k req/s (×5 peak ≈ 5k)
Concurrency (Little's Law): 1k × 10 s = 10k open streams (×5 ≈ 50k SSE conns) — size the connection plane by this, not QPS.
Tokens: 100M × 1.5k = 150B/day (100B in + 50B out).
Cost: 100B×$1/M + 50B×$4/M = $100k + $200k ≈ $300k/day (~$110M/yr).
Headline: ~10k concurrent streams (50k peak) is the scaling unit; ~150B tokens/day ≈ ~$300k/day.

prompts.prompt: Size the ingest QPS, read QPS, and storage for a trending / top-K over an event stream (e.g. trending hashtags), stating your assumptions.
prompts.answer:
Assume: 200M DAU, 5 tagged actions/user/day (1B/day), count per (tag, 1-min window), keep top-1000, panel cached 30 s.
Ingest: 1B ÷ 100k ≈ 10k events/s (×5 peak ≈ 50k)
Reads: 200M × 10 panel loads = 2B/day ÷ 100k ≈ 20k reads/s → 30 s cache TTL collapses origin to ~hundreds/s.
Storage: ~10M distinct tags/window × 16 B ≈ 160 MB/window in memory; rollups ~50 GB/day durable.
Headline: ~10k events/s in, ~20k reads/s cache-served; sharded windowed counters plus a top-K heap — hot tags need cell-sharded counts.

prompts.prompt: How does Postgres handle an UPDATE at the storage level, and why does that matter for readers?
prompts.answer: Postgres uses MVCC and does NOT update in place: an UPDATE writes a new row version and marks the old one dead, so readers get a consistent snapshot without blocking writers. VACUUM later reclaims the dead versions.

prompts.prompt: What is the single most common real-world Postgres scaling gotcha, and does it hit before or after raw throughput limits?
prompts.answer: Connection exhaustion: each connection is roughly a backend process consuming megabytes of RAM, so a few thousand direct connections exhaust it well before you run out of raw throughput. Put PgBouncer (or equivalent) in front.

prompts.prompt: Name Postgres's three durability layers and the distinct failure each one survives.
prompts.answer: Local WAL fsync survives a crash (power loss/panic) but not disk/node loss; synchronous replication (ANY 1 of several standbys, ideally another AZ) survives node loss so no acknowledged write lives on a single disk; WAL archiving + PITR survives logical corruption (a bad DELETE replicates faithfully, only point-in-time recovery saves you).

prompts.prompt: Why is Cassandra a terrible choice for a queue or high-churn delete workload?
prompts.answer: Deletes write tombstones (markers) rather than removing data, and they linger until compaction; reading across many tombstones craters latency, so write-then-delete queue churn punishes you.

prompts.prompt: CAP line: Cassandra is AP by design but tunable toward CP. What exact quorum config gives strong reads, and what consistency does it still NOT provide?
prompts.answer: QUORUM reads + QUORUM writes satisfy R + W > N, so the read overlaps the latest write for strong consistency. Even at ALL you only get replication consistency, never transactional — there's no 'update these three rows or none' and LWT is single-partition compare-and-set only.

prompts.prompt: Modern Redis uses I/O threads — so is command execution still atomic, and what's the load-bearing property?
prompts.answer: Yes: I/O threads only handle network, but actual command (and Lua script) execution stays serialized/single-threaded, so every op runs atomically with no locks — the property that makes it right for admission control and rate limiting.

prompts.prompt: Name the default Redis caching pattern and how you mitigate a hot key expiring under load.
prompts.answer: Cache-aside (lazy): app checks cache, on miss reads DB and populates. For a hot key expiring — cache stampede / thundering herd — mitigate with a short lock around the refill so one request repopulates, request coalescing, or probabilistic early expiry.

prompts.prompt: Redis TTL hold vs a Postgres DB sweeper: what's the deciding factor for which one to use?
prompts.answer: Redis TTL only wins if the key IS the hold (its disappearance is the release), fit for ticket-onsale scale like 100k holds/s with a visible countdown. If Postgres owns the counter, a DB sweeper beats Redis keyspace notifications — durable and self-healing (notifications are at-most-once).

prompts.prompt: In a Kafka consumer group, what caps parallelism, and what happens to processing when a consumer joins or leaves?
prompts.answer: Partition count caps parallelism — consumers ≤ partitions, so extra consumers sit idle. A join/leave triggers consumer-group rebalancing, which reassigns partitions and briefly pauses (stop-the-world) processing; frequent rebalances are a classic incident.

prompts.prompt: CAP/consistency line: Kafka's exactly-once semantics apply to what exactly, and what do they NOT cover?
prompts.answer: Exactly-once (EOS) applies only within Kafka — read-process-write across Kafka topics. It does not extend to external side effects like your DB write or an API call; delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must still be idempotent.

prompts.prompt: State the rule of thumb for choosing a Kafka log vs a task queue (SQS/RabbitMQ).
prompts.answer: Need replay or multiple independent consumers of the same event → log (Kafka: retained, rewindable, fan-out). Need work distribution with per-message retry/DLQ → queue (consumed-and-deleted, ack/redelivery, competing consumers, no replay).

prompts.prompt: Walk through what happens to a message in a task queue from delivery through failure handling.
prompts.answer: A worker pulls a message, processes it, and acks to delete it. No ack (crash/timeout) makes it visible again and it's redelivered after the visibility timeout; after N failed attempts it goes to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for inspection. Once consumed and acked it's gone — no offset to rewind, no replay.

prompts.prompt: Cassandra vs sharded Postgres: at your volume, what is Cassandra's actual edge — and when should you just use Postgres?
prompts.answer: The edge isn't write throughput — it's that consistent hashing makes rebalancing automatic and multi-region replication a config line, not a project. Below genuine global scale Postgres is the better default even for keyed data, keeping transactions and query flexibility; Cassandra wins only when scale × geo-distribution × access-pattern-simplicity all hold at once.

prompts.prompt: CAP/consistency line: what is S3's consistency model today, and what are its real limits?
prompts.answer: S3 is strongly read-after-write consistent for all operations (since Dec 2020) — a GET after a PUT returns the latest object. Don't cite the old eventual-consistency caveat; the real limits are no cross-object transactions and no querying inside objects — it's a durable key→blob store, not a database.

prompts.prompt: Describe the presigned direct upload and multipart patterns for S3, including the key numbers.
prompts.answer: Presigned direct upload: the client PUTs straight to S3 with a time-limited signed URL, so bytes bypass your API tier. Multipart splits big files into parts (one presigned URL per part, parallel, per-part retry, resumable via ListParts) — 5 MB part minimum, 10k parts max, and single PUT caps at 5 GB.

prompts.prompt: CAP/consistency line: why is a CDN deliberately eventually consistent, and what's the right way to reason about it?
prompts.answer: The edge serves possibly-stale content bounded by TTL, and that staleness IS the tradeoff you accept for latency and origin offload. Design around what's cacheable and for how long — lean on short TTLs over active purge — not how to make the edge fresh.

prompts.prompt: For a vector DB, what's the real deployment gotcha, and how do you fit a large corpus in RAM?
prompts.answer: The HNSW graph memory frequently exceeds the raw vectors, so the deployed memory footprint is the gotcha (e.g. 1M × 1536-dim is ~6 GB raw plus the graph). Quantization fits large corpora: int8 ~4× smaller, binary ~32×.

prompts.prompt: Vector-only vs hybrid retrieval: when does pure vector search fail, and what's the sharp permission failure mode?
prompts.answer: Pure semantic search misses exact terms (names, IDs, codes), so hybrid BM25 + vector often wins. The sharp failure is permission leakage: embeddings ignore ACLs, so you must filter by permission (ACL) at query time or you retrieve across tenants.

prompts.prompt: A workflow orchestrator gives exactly-once continuation on top of what activity guarantee, and how does its fan-in avoid a counter race?
prompts.answer: Exactly-once continuation layers on at-least-once activity execution, so activities must still be idempotent. Fan-in is a read over the ordered durable history log decided by a single evaluator ('is there a completion for every scheduled task'), so there's no concurrent-counter race by construction.

prompts.prompt: The Elasticsearch-as-database trap: why is it wrong, and what is ES's actual role?
prompts.answer: It's a derived read model, not a source of truth — near-real-time (~1s refresh), no ACID/transactions, and eventually consistent with your primary by construction. Feed it from the primary via CDC, design a reconciliation path, and be able to rebuild the index from truth at any time.

prompts.prompt: State the decision-matrix meta-rule for how most systems are composed and what signals coherence.
prompts.answer: Most systems are Postgres + one or two specialists: Postgres as the transactional source of truth plus a cache (Redis), blob store (S3), CDN, and maybe a search/vector index fed via CDC. Reach for Cassandra/Kafka/an orchestrator only when a named requirement forces it; naming the one store as truth and treating the rest as derived is the coherence signal.

prompts.prompt: What cross-cutting asymmetry sits behind CDNs, read replicas, caches, and search indexes — and when do you move a guarantee out of the DB?
prompts.answer: Reads tolerate staleness; writes must be correct. Move a guarantee out of the database only when arrival rate makes the DB physically unable to provide it — the same rule for sharding, Redis holds, and counter offloading.

prompts.prompt: What is the one thing you must get right when modeling a DynamoDB table, and what breaks if you don’t?
prompts.answer: The partition key must be high-cardinality and evenly accessed. A skewed key (one celebrity, one tenant) creates a hot partition that throttles — even when the table has spare total capacity. Same failure class as a Cassandra hot partition.

prompts.prompt: DynamoDB reads: what is the default consistency, and how do you get strong consistency?
prompts.answer: Reads default to eventually consistent (cheaper, from any replica). You opt into strongly consistent reads per request (more cost, leader replica, single-region only). Global tables are last-writer-wins and eventually consistent across regions — no cross-region strong consistency.

prompts.prompt: DynamoDB vs Cassandra — how do you actually decide between them?
prompts.answer: Mostly buy vs run: same Dynamo data model and tradeoffs. DynamoDB is managed/serverless with per-request pricing and zero ops; Cassandra is self-hosted with a fixed cluster cost. Both demand partition-key discipline and forbid joins/cheap cross-partition transactions.

prompts.prompt: What are DynamoDB’s item-size and transaction limits, and how do they shape your design?
prompts.answer: Item cap is 400 KB — large blobs go to S3 with the key stored in Dynamo. TransactWriteItems caps at 25 items and costs ~2× throughput. So you model access patterns into composite keys (single-table design) and design reads as key lookups; never build around Scan.

prompts.prompt: Kafka moves the stream — what does Flink add, and when do you need it?
prompts.answer: Flink is stateful compute over the stream: windowed aggregations, stream joins, sessionization, real-time pattern detection. Kafka moves and retains; Flink windows, aggregates, and joins. Reach for it when you need to compute over the stream, not just transport it — not a hand-rolled consumer with a counter.

prompts.prompt: In Flink, what is the difference between event-time and processing-time, and what makes event-time correct?
prompts.answer: Event-time uses the event’s own timestamp plus watermarks (a watermark asserts “no more events older than T”) so late and out-of-order events still land in the right window. Processing-time uses the wall clock — simpler but wrong under lateness. Naming watermarks is the signal.

prompts.prompt: How does Flink achieve exactly-once, and what is the catch?
prompts.answer: Distributed checkpointing: Chandy–Lamport barriers flow through the graph and snapshot each operator’s state; on failure the job rewinds to the last checkpoint and replays from the source offset → exactly-once state. Catch: end-to-end exactly-once needs a transactional/idempotent sink; otherwise the output is at-least-once.

prompts.prompt: What is ZooKeeper/etcd for, and what should you never use it for?
prompts.answer: Consensus-backed coordination for small metadata: leader election, distributed locks, membership, consistent config that pushes changes to watchers. Never a data store or high-throughput write path — it holds kilobytes per node in memory, and every write is a quorum consensus round.

prompts.prompt: Name ZooKeeper’s three primitives and what each one enables.
prompts.answer: Ephemeral nodes vanish when a client’s session heartbeat lapses → liveness/membership. Watches notify clients on change → config push and leader-change notification. Sequential nodes give globally ordered names → fair locks and leader election.

prompts.prompt: Why is a ZooKeeper/etcd lock “more correct” than a Redis lock?
prompts.answer: ZooKeeper/etcd commit writes on quorum consensus (CP), so a minority partition cannot take the lock — no split-brain. A Redis lock is a best-effort lease (availability-first, safe only with a fencing token). Use consensus when a double-holder is a correctness bug, not a nuisance.

prompts.prompt: Why is ZooKeeper/etcd CP, and what does that cost you during a partition?
prompts.answer: Writes commit only on a quorum (majority) via ZAB/Raft; a 2f+1 ensemble tolerates f failures. During a partition the minority side stops accepting writes rather than risk split-brain — you lose availability there, which is exactly what you want backing a lock or leader election.

prompts.prompt: At what write throughput to a single Postgres table should you consider sharding or moving off — and what do you do before that?
prompts.answer: Under ~5k writes/s: fine, don’t move. ~5k–15k/s: tune first — batch inserts, offload the hot counter to Redis, faster-fsync disk, fewer indexes. ~15k–50k/s: shard by a good key (keep SQL/transactions within a shard). >~50k/s, an append-only firehose, or multi-region writes: move the hot table to an LSM/wide-column store (Cassandra/DynamoDB) or a TSDB.

prompts.prompt: A global counter or inventory row is the bottleneck at a few hundred writes/s while the rest of the table is fine — what’s happening, and what do you do?
prompts.answer: A single hot row hits row-lock contention (ceiling ~500–1k serialized updates/s), not table throughput. Offload that one value to Redis INCR or shard the counter; the rest of the table stays in Postgres. It’s the row, not the table size.

prompts.prompt: What actually forces you off a single Postgres primary — is it database size?
prompts.answer: Almost never aggregate size (100M+ rows on one primary is routine). It’s a specific hot table (past ~15–50k writes/s), a single hot row (past ~500–1k/s), an append-only firehose, or active-active multi-region writes — the write pattern, not the row count. Connection exhaustion also hits first; pool with PgBouncer before touching architecture.

prompts.prompt: Walk the ChatGPT-like send path from client POST to model, naming each component in order.
prompts.answer: Client POST -> gateway (auth, per-user rate/token quota) -> chat service persists the user message plus an assistant-message placeholder (status: generating) -> context builder (system policy + recent turns + summary + ACL-filtered retrieval, packed to token budget) -> inference orchestrator (routing, admission queue, streaming) -> provider/model pool.

prompts.prompt: In a ChatGPT-like system, where does conversation state actually live, and what is the retrieval index/summaries' relationship to it?
prompts.answer: The conversation store is the single source of truth; the retrieval index, summaries, and analytics are all rebuildable projections derived from it.

prompts.prompt: When streaming tokens back, at what granularity does the orchestrator write chunks to the persisted placeholder, and what is saved on completion?
prompts.answer: It appends chunks with buffered writes, not one write per token, and on completion persists the final text plus usage and finish reason.

prompts.prompt: Name the stages of the RAG query pipeline in order.
prompts.answer: Authorization filter -> lexical + vector retrieval -> dedupe -> rerank -> context pack (to token budget) -> generate with citations.

prompts.prompt: State where LLM latency actually splits, and why the cost unit is asymmetric.
prompts.answer: Latency = time-to-first-token (queueing + prefill, which grows with prompt length) plus decode (commonly tens of tokens/sec per stream); cost is per token with output tokens typically costing several times input tokens, and long context inflates both cost and TTFT.

prompts.prompt: To exploit prefix/prompt caching, how must you order the context, and which levers do you pull before changing model choice?
prompts.answer: Put the stable part (system prompt + tools prefix) first so the provider can cache it; trim, summarize, and cap output length before touching model choice, and track cost per successful outcome rather than per request.

prompts.prompt: How should RAG evals be structured, including the no-ground-truth case, and what config must be versioned?
prompts.answer: Evaluate retrieval separately (recall@k, ranking, freshness, permission leakage) then answer groundedness and task success, using deterministic checks where possible, calibrated model graders where there is no ground truth, and human review for high-impact quality; version the model, prompt, tools, retrieval config, safety policy, and response schema as production artifacts.

prompts.prompt: State the core prompt-injection defense principle and name three concrete guardrails.
prompts.answer: Separate trusted instructions from untrusted retrieved/user content so documents cannot grant tool authority; guardrails include least-privilege scoped-credential tools, sandboxing with network/domain restrictions, and confirmation gates before high-impact actions.

prompts.prompt: In single-leader replication, what is split-brain and how is it typically prevented during failover?
prompts.answer: Split-brain is when two nodes both believe they are leader after a failover, causing conflicting writes and data corruption. It's prevented by requiring a quorum/majority to elect a leader, fencing tokens, and STONITH-style shutdown of the old leader.

prompts.prompt: What is replication lag, and how does 'read-your-writes' consistency address one of its problems?
prompts.answer: Replication lag is the delay before an async follower reflects a leader's write, so a fresh read from a follower can miss the user's own recent write. Read-your-writes guarantees a user always sees their own updates, e.g. by reading from the leader (or a monitored recent follower) for data they may have modified.

prompts.prompt: What causes a hot partition (hot spot), and what's a common mitigation?
prompts.answer: A hot partition occurs when a skewed access pattern concentrates load on one key or key range (e.g. a celebrity user or monotonic timestamp key). Mitigations include hashing the key to spread load, or adding a random/derived prefix to a hot key and fanning reads across the split.

prompts.prompt: Why is hash-mod-N a poor rebalancing strategy, and what is used instead?
prompts.answer: mod N remaps almost every key when N changes, forcing massive data movement. Instead use a fixed large number of partitions assigned to nodes, consistent hashing, or dynamic partitioning that splits/merges by size — so adding a node moves only a small fraction of data.

prompts.prompt: Contrast linearizability with eventual consistency.
prompts.answer: Linearizability is a strong recency guarantee: the system behaves as if there is one copy and every operation takes effect atomically at a point between its start and end, so a read always returns the latest committed write. Eventual consistency only guarantees replicas converge if writes stop, allowing stale reads in the meantime.

prompts.prompt: In a quorum system, why is R + W > N the key inequality, and what does it guarantee?
prompts.answer: With N replicas, W nodes acked on write and R nodes read, R + W > N forces the read set and write set to overlap in at least one node, so a read sees the latest write. It does not by itself provide linearizability due to races, sloppy quorums, and concurrent writes.

prompts.prompt: State the CAP theorem precisely and what PACELC adds.
prompts.answer: CAP: when a network partition occurs, a system must choose between consistency (linearizability) and availability; it cannot have both during the partition. PACELC extends it: even when there is no partition (Else), you trade Latency versus Consistency.

prompts.prompt: Name the read anomalies each isolation level prevents: read committed, snapshot isolation, serializable.
prompts.answer: Read committed prevents dirty reads and dirty writes. Snapshot isolation (repeatable read) additionally prevents non-repeatable reads via a consistent snapshot (MVCC) but still allows write skew and phantoms. Serializable prevents all of these, including write skew and phantoms.

prompts.prompt: What is write skew, and why doesn't snapshot isolation prevent it?
prompts.answer: Write skew is when two transactions read the same overlapping data, then each updates a different row, and together they violate an invariant (e.g. both on-call doctors book off because each saw the other still on). Snapshot isolation checks only for write-write conflicts on the same rows, so disjoint writes based on a stale premise slip through; you need serializable isolation (SSI) or explicit locking.

prompts.prompt: Why is distributed consensus (e.g. leader election) fundamentally hard?
prompts.answer: In an asynchronous network you cannot distinguish a crashed node from a slow one or a dropped message, so agreement must tolerate arbitrary delays and partitions; the FLP result shows no deterministic algorithm guarantees consensus with even one faulty node without timeouts. Practical protocols like Raft/Paxos use majority quorums, terms/epochs, and randomized timeouts to make progress safely.

prompts.prompt: What is idempotency and why is it the practical basis for 'exactly-once' processing?
prompts.answer: An idempotent operation produces the same result whether applied once or many times, so a client can safely retry after an uncertain outcome. True exactly-once delivery is impossible over unreliable networks, so systems achieve exactly-once effects by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent operations or dedup via unique request IDs.

prompts.prompt: Compare LSM-trees and B-trees on write path and read/space tradeoffs.
prompts.answer: LSM-trees batch writes in memory and flush sequential sorted segments compacted in the background, giving high write throughput and good compression but read amplification and compaction-induced write amplification/latency spikes. B-trees update pages in place (often with a WAL), giving predictable reads and strong transactional locality but more random I/O and typically lower write throughput.

prompts.prompt: Tell me about a zero-to-one project you drove from nothing to production.
prompts.answer: STAR: frame the ambiguity/absence of a spec, then YOUR decisions on scope, tech, and cut-lines to ship a v1. Land on the first real user/metric outcome and what you deliberately deferred to get there.

prompts.prompt: Describe a significant conflict with another team and how you resolved it.
prompts.answer: STAR: name the competing goals/incentives, not personalities. Show you sought the other team's constraints, proposed a shared success metric, and drove a durable agreement — end with the mechanism that prevented recurrence.

prompts.prompt: Tell me about a time you were wrong about something technical or strategic.
prompts.answer: STAR: state your original position and the evidence that changed your mind. Land on how quickly you reversed, what it cost, and the systemic change (a check, a review, a default) you added so the class of error doesn't repeat.

prompts.prompt: Walk me through shipping something under heavy ambiguity and a hard deadline.
prompts.answer: STAR: surface the unknowns explicitly and how you reduced them (spikes, assumptions, reversible decisions). Land on what you cut, the tradeoff you owned, and the concrete outcome — decisiveness under uncertainty, not paralysis.

prompts.prompt: Give an example of influencing a major technical direction without formal authority.
prompts.answer: STAR: show how you built the case — data, a prototype, aligning stakeholders one-on-one before the room. Land on the decision changing because of your work and name who you moved and how, not just that you were right.

prompts.prompt: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision but had to commit to it.
prompts.answer: STAR: articulate your objection crisply and where you raised it, then show disagree-and-commit — you executed fully and in good faith. Land on the outcome and what you learned about when to escalate versus support.

prompts.prompt: Describe how you mentored or grew an engineer to the next level.
prompts.answer: STAR: identify the specific gap and the deliberate plan (stretch work, feedback cadence, sponsorship). Land on the measurable growth outcome — a promotion, ownership handed off, or capability the team now has because of you.

prompts.prompt: Tell me about a serious failure or production outage you owned.
prompts.answer: STAR: take clear ownership, walk the detection-to-mitigation timeline and your role in it. Land on the blameless root cause and the concrete systemic fixes (tests, alerts, guardrails) plus impact reduced — accountability over excuses.

prompts.prompt: Why this company, and why this role at this point in your career?
prompts.answer: Connect a specific company problem/mission to your proven strengths and what you want to grow next; be concrete about their product or tech, not generic. Land on the unique value you'd add and why the timing fits both sides.

prompts.prompt: Pick your most technically challenging project and go deep on the hardest decision.
prompts.answer: Set minimal context fast, then spend the time on ONE hard tradeoff: the options, your evaluation criteria, why you chose, and how it played out. Land on YOUR reasoning and measurable impact, showing depth an interviewer can probe.
